newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Xmas ceasefire in Creditanstalt battle.
newsitem.headline: Xmas ceasefire in Creditanstalt battle.

text.p: Austria's coalition government began an uneasy Christmas truce on Tuesday, postponing its next move in the tortuous sale of number two bank Creditanstalt Bankverein until after the holiday.
With Austrian markets and most offices closed for three days, few expected any new developments in Europe's longest running privatisation before Friday at the earliest.

Then Finance Minister Viktor Klima, charged with the sale of the state's 70 percent of Creditanstalt voting stock, could reopen the tender briefly to allow interested parties to top up their offers without drawing in new partners.
That would allow him to wrap up the six-year privatisation by the end of the year as originally planned.
But a finance ministry source said the fragility of the coalition of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party meant Klima was likely to tread carefully and seek a consensus.
That would mean delaying the sale until mid-January.
"In theory, Klima could accept top-up bids on December 27 and decide on a buyer on December 30...But a postponement is looking increasingly likely," the source said late on Monday.
"The Finance Minister is under intense political pressure (to delay the sale)," he added.
Politics have dominated the privatisation of conservative stronghold Creditanstalt since it was first mooted in 1990.
The People's Party and Creditanstalt management have sought to protect their interests by opposing "unsuitable" bids from abroad and, most recently, from "socialist" Bank Austria.
Social Democrat Klima, who took over the finance portfolio a year ago, has argued his hands are tied by EU legislation that requires him to sell to the highest bidder - market leader Bank Austria.
Analysts say a conservative-backed consortium, led by insurer EA-Generali, would be the biggest gainer if Klima did reopen the bidding.

The group, which includes savings bank Die Erste Oesterreichische SparCasse (First Austrian), Germany's Commerzbank and Italy's Banca Commerciale Italiana, is reportedly trying to drum up an extra three billion schillings ($274.7 million) to match Bank Austria.
Bank Austria has put up some 16 billion schillings for the state's 19.9 million shares, worth about 14 billion schillings at current market prices.

"The whole thing has become very complicated. If Klima awards the stake to Bank Austria he risks causing a new election, which the Social Democrats don't want," said Gerhard Auer, analyst at ICE Securities in London. "He needs some time to persuade the consortium to offer a bit more."

The finance ministry source said negotiations were going on at all levels of government. Analysts say the conservatives will be looking for concessions elsewhere if they agree to a Bank Austria takeover of Creditanstalt.
In a newspaper interview Bank Austria chief executive Gerhard Randa vented his frustration at what he considers political gerrymandering in the sale.

"I don't get involved in politics and I wish politics would keep out of the banking business," he told Die Presse. "I remain convinced that Bank Austria offers the best solution for Austrian banking and this change is necessary in the light of European integration and the future euro."
